name: Thule people
title: The story of the Thule people

text: About 1,000 years ago, the Thule people lived on the coasts of Alaska.
They were the ancestors of the Inuit and Yupik peoples.
src: Arctic hunters who developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE
The Thule were the direct ancestors of the Inuit and Yupik

text: They hunted bowhead whales from boats made of skins, with crews working together under a captain.
One whale gave meat for food, blubber for light and bone for houses and tools.
src: Their life centred on bowhead whaling from skin boats / hunted by cooperating boat crews under a captain, the umialik
A single whale gave meat for food, blubber for light and cooking, and bone for houses and tools

text: With dog sleds, kayaks and skin boats, they spread across northern Canada to Greenland.
There they took the place of the Dorset people, who had lived there before.
src: Dog sleds, kayaks and large skin boats let the Thule range far / within a few centuries spread across northern Canada to Greenland
the Thule displaced the Dorset people who had occupied the central and eastern Canadian Arctic

text: They made knives of polished slate, and passed copper and iron from community to community.
Some iron came from meteorites, rocks from the sky, and some from trade with the Norse.
src: Tool kits were dominated by polished slate rather than flaked stone: lance-shaped knives / native copper from the western Arctic and meteoric iron from north-western Greenland passed from community to community
some came from meteorites, such as the Cape York meteorite in Greenland, and some through trade from the Norse

text: Later, a colder climate brought fewer whales, and the old whaling life broke up.
Their descendants are today’s Inuit and Yupik, and whaling captains are still important in Alaska.
src: A colder period between 1400 and 1600 limited the use of boats, reduced the number of whales / A colder climate after 1400 broke up the old whaling life
their descendants are the Inuit and Yupik of today / the umialik, the whaling captain of Thule times, is still a prominent figure in Alaskan Arctic communities
